title: Luna, the Flame Spirit of Flemish Hearths
summary: A gentle household spirit who protects Flemish hearths but punishes those who let the fire die out of laziness.
full_text:
In the farmhouses of old Flanders, where the winter wind howls across the polders and the canals freeze solid, the hearth was the heart of the home. And every hearth had its guardian. Luna, the flame spirit, was said to live within the embers, a being of warmth and light no larger than a thumb. She slept in the ash by day and danced in the flames by night.

The family who kept a clean hearth and fed the fire faithfully would find their home blessed. Their bread rose higher, their beer stayed sweeter, and their children never woke from nightmares. Luna would sing in the crackling fire, a sound like distant bells, and those who heard it slept deeply and dreamed of summer. But Luna was no passive servant. She demanded respect. A farmer named Klaas, known for his laziness, let his fire sink to embers one bitter January night rather than fetch more wood from the shed. In the morning, the fire was stone cold, and so was Klaas's heart. He fell ill, and his fields yielded nothing that year.

The old women of the village knew how to keep Luna happy. They swept the hearth every morning, sprinkled a pinch of salt into the flames, and never let the fire go out completely. On St. Martin's Eve, they left a small cup of milk by the fireplace. In return, Luna kept their homes warm through the darkest months. Some say Luna is still there, in the old farmhouses of Flanders, waiting for someone to light a fire and remember the old ways.
moral: Neglect of the small duties invites the greatest losses.

title: L'Ankou, the Dark Coachman of the Low Countries
summary: A death omen spirit who drives a ghostly coach across the Belgian countryside, collecting the souls of those about to die.
full_text:
When the fog rolls in from the North Sea and blankets the fields of Wallonia, those who live in the old stone farmhouses lock their doors and say their prayers. For in that fog, they know, drives L'Ankou, the dark coachman. His coach is made of bones and shadow, pulled by two headless horses whose hooves make no sound. The wheels creak like the hinges of a tomb, and the lantern that swings from his coach burns with a pale blue light that freezes the blood.

L'Ankou is not a demon in the Christian sense. He is older than that, a figure from the ancient beliefs of the Celtic peoples who once inhabited these lands. He is the gatherer of souls, the last companion on every journey. When a person's time comes, L'Ankou appears at the end of their road, silent and patient. He offers no violence, no demands. He simply opens the door of his coach, and the soul steps inside. The ride is short, for the journey is not measured in miles.

A young priest from Namur once tried to exorcise L'Ankou, standing in the fog with a cross and a vial of holy water. The coach emerged from the mist and stopped before him. L'Ankou leaned out, his face hidden beneath a wide hat, and spoke: 'I am no devil to be banished. I am the end of all things. You cannot exorcise death.' The priest dropped his cross and fled. He served in a small parish for the rest of his days and never spoke of the encounter.

In Walloon tradition, hearing the creak of L'Ankou's wheels means someone in the village will die within three days. It is not a curse. It is a warning, a chance to make peace with God and with men.
moral: Death comes for all; live so that you are ready.

title: The Kabouter of the Belgian Forests
summary: A tiny forest spirit who helps those who respect nature and plays tricks on those who do not, found in the woods of Flanders.
full_text:
The Kabouter is a small, bearded man no taller than a mushroom, dressed in green clothes and a red pointed hat. He lives in the forests of Flanders, under the roots of ancient oaks, in houses built of acorn caps and moss. The Kabouter is a creature of the old world, a remnant of the time when spirits walked openly among men.

Kabouters are generally friendly, helpful to those who treat the forest with care. A farmer who left a bowl of milk at the edge of the woods might find his fields tilled by morning. A woodcutter who thanked the trees before cutting them would never lack good timber. But the Kabouter's kindness had limits. Those who harmed the forest for sport, who broke branches for no reason, who killed birds or trampled mushrooms, would find their tools broken, their paths confused, and their livestock scattered.

A miller named Willem once captured a Kabouter and kept him in a cage, demanding that the little creature grind his grain forever. The Kabouter said nothing for three days. On the third night, every mill in the valley began to turn by itself, the great wheels spinning so fast that sparks flew from the stones. The noise was deafening, and the villagers gathered in terror. Willem opened the cage, and the Kabouter walked out without a backward glance. The mills fell silent. But Willem's mill never worked properly again.

The Kabouters are still there, in the old forests of Flanders. If you walk quietly and listen closely, you might hear their tiny footsteps, like the rustle of leaves, following you through the trees.
moral: Freedom is not a gift to be taken; it is a right to be respected.

title: Cheval Mal Fet, the Cursed Steed
summary: A ghostly black horse that appears on the roads of Wallonia, carrying a demonic rider who tempts travelers into deadly bargains.
full_text:
On the dark roads of Wallonia, where the villages are few and the lanterns are far between, there sometimes appears a horse of terrifying beauty. The Cheval Mal Fet is blacker than midnight, with eyes that burn like coals and breath that steams in the cold air. Its rider is a shadow, a demon in human form, dressed in fine clothes but with no face beneath his hat.

The horse appears to travelers who are tired and desperate, those who have walked too far and still have miles to go. The demon rider offers a ride. 'Get on,' he says, his voice smooth as silk. 'I will take you where you need to go.' The traveler who accepts finds himself flying down the road at impossible speed. Trees blur past. The wind screams. But the ride never ends. The horse runs until dawn, and when the first light breaks, the traveler finds himself alone at the crossroads, having traded something precious for the ride: his memory, his voice, or ten years of his life.

A merchant named Jean from Arlon accepted the ride on a winter night. He arrived at his destination in minutes instead of hours, but from that day forward, he could not remember his own name. He wandered the streets of his town, a stranger to his wife and children, until one day he walked into the forest and was never seen again. The village priest warned that the Cheval Mal Fet is a temptation of the devil, a shortcut that always ends in damnation. Better to walk, he said, than to ride with demons.

To this day, Walloon parents warn their children: if you hear hooves on a lonely road at night, step into the ditch and do not look up.
moral: There are no shortcuts in life that do not exact a price.
